newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup: Taking credit.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup: Taking credit.

text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)
If you like a good laugh it's hard to top the sophistry which passes for economic debate in federal parliament and its environs.

The first months of a new government provide rich pickings for economic double-speak as the new incumbents of the Treasury benches take credit for all the glad tidings while lambasting the former administration for the less welcome statistical trends.
At the same time the new opposition reverses the process.
This week has given us some prime examples of this high art.

Take shadow employment minister Martin Ferguson's question on Monday: "Is the prime minister aware that today's ANZ job survey shows that job advertisements have now fallen for four consecutive months, for the first time in nearly five years and that jobs growth is only half the rate needed to meet modest budget forecasts of employment growth?"

Not bad from Martin, given that he would surely know the labour market provides a lagging indicator to general economic activity and is just as likely to reflect conditions at the end of Labor's reign as much as the early months of the coalition.
That didn't escape the prime minister, however.
"Let everybody understand that we have been in office for eight months yet it is all our fault. They were there for 13 years and none of it is their fault. It is an extraordinary proposition."
Yet in the very next question -- a Dorothy Dixer -- Treasurer Peter Costello took a very different approach to an improvement in home loan affordability.

"It gives this side of the house great encouragement to see that we are delivering housing affordability in the September quarter," claiming that "It is sound economic policy which has made housing affordability so great for the average Australian family."
All with typical Costello bravura and not a hint of a blush.

Just to show nothing can embarrass the treasurer, Costello was up a couple of questions later, complaining: "Every time there is a good inflation figure, Senator (Nick) Sherry (opposition finance spokesman) runs out and says, 'It's all Labor's doing.' Every time there is a retail figure, you run out and say 'It's the coalition's doing.' One of the things you will have to do is get some consistency. You have to actually understand. The trouble is where there is no understanding there is no conscience."

And that was a platform for Wednesday's interest rate cut which saw Costello let himself go, quite forgetting it wasn't so long ago he signed a letter with new Reserve Bank Governor Ian Macfarlane cementing the bank's independence.

"This is a government that said it would stand by the battlers and the families of Australia; and today this government delivers again. This government has now delivered a 1.75 percent reduction, A$145 a month -- after tax -- on the average mortgage to the average Australian family."

Both Costello and John Howard also congratulated themselves on three percent economic growth as being "strong growth" and near the top of the OECD league, putting aside the fact that the economy was growing at three percent before the election when Howard was complaining of "five minutes of economic sunshine."
But the opposition treasury spokesman scores well in the double-speak event too.

Gareth Evans had a news conference on the interest rate cuts, claiming it was a rescue for a flat economy, not a reward for good coalition policy. A journalist was impertinent enough to ask: "But Mr Evans, last time there was a rate cut the opposition claimed it as your rate cut and you said it was your figures and your strategy that had put that in place. Now it's because the economy is as flat as a billiard table. Is that because of you as well?"

This was Evans' reply: "We were the ones that broke inflation in this country, we broke the back of inflationary expectations and it continues to be our legacy that has created the underlying conditions for the last rate cut and indeed for this one. But the dynamic that's applying to this particular rate cut is very different from that which was prevailing back in March, April, May. What we now have is an economy that has dramatically slowed as compared to the rate at which it was rolling along at the time of the change of government, and an economy which every indicator is pointing to further serious concerns about."
Is it any wonder the place is awash with cynicism?
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau, 61-6 273-2730
